citeinfo.title: High spatial resolution sensor-based surface water quality data along the Lake Winnebago-Fox River-Green Bay continuum in 2023-2025

descript.abstract:
In support of multiple Great Lakes Restoration Initiative (GLRI) projects focusing on Green Bay and upland sources, surface water quality metrics related to primary producers, nutrients, and conductivity were measured using a boat-mounted, continuous sampling platform. These data are used to document changes in water quality as water flows from Lake Winnebago through the lower Fox River and ultimately into Green Bay. Surface water quality was measured using a boat-mounted, continuous sampling platform known as the Fast Limnological Automated Measurements (FLAMe; https://doi.org/10.1021/es504773x). Water was continually pumped onboard a moving boat to a series of water quality sensors configured to capture data continuously. Measurements were georeferenced and spatially corrected using established routines and can be used to produce maps of water quality where the boat traveled. Overall, 455,102 point measurements were collected across the inland water continuum (available in file: FLAMe_data.csv). Additionally, sensor-based measurements are associated with 239 discrete field measurements and/or water samples analyzed for additional chemical and biological attributes (available in file: FLAMe_samples.csv).
Up to nine onboard multiparameter instruments recording data from one or more sensors were used to collect up to 82 variables during eight sampling campaigns between August 2023 and July 2025. Onboard water quality sensors varied among campaigns, and included a YSI EXO2 (temperature, specific conductivity, turbidity, pH, dissolved oxygen, dissolved organic matter fluorescence, and total algal fluorescence), a Seabird SUNA V2 optical nitrate sensor (nitrate, absorbance), a bbe fluoroprobe (green algae, blue green algae, diatoms, and cryptophytes), and a Los Gatos Research Ultraportable Greenhouse Gas Analyzer (dissolved carbon dioxide and methane). Additional instruments included two Garmin Global Positioning System (GPS) receivers (latitude, longitude, time), a Garmin depth sounder (water temperature and depth), and a Vaisala CS106 barometer (barometric pressure). All data were recorded continuously on a Campbell Scientific CR6 datalogger. System attributes (e.g., internal temperature, boat speed, wiper position, battery voltage) were also recorded to aid data quality control. Details on data attributes including descriptions, units, and sources are included in the file: FLAMe_data_dictionary.csv.
This data release contains spatial data from three overlapping GLRI-funded research projects focused in Lake Winnebago, the lower Fox River, and Green Bay using common equipment. Six 3- to 4-day campaigns (August 2023, June 2024, July 2024, August 2024, May 2025, and July 2025) targeted phytoplankton distribution in the Lake Winnebago-Fox River-Green Bay continuum. Spatial transects were established crossing the north-half of Lake Winnebago, along the Fox River, and out into Green Bay. Two additional 2- to 3-day campaigns (April 2025, June 2025) focused on salinity patterns in Green Bay with 14 littoral/pelagic transects circumnavigating Green Bay from Marinette, WI to Brussels, WI. The crew attempted to sample the same features on each campaign; however, the exact sample path varied based on weather and hydrologic conditions. Actual sampling locations loosely followed pre-determined routes, but they were adjusted based on weather, field observations, and communication with local guides. See file: FLAMe_map.png for transect paths organized by campaign.
descript.purpose: These data were collected to evaluate spatial patterns in phytoplankton, nutrients, salinity, and other water quality parameters in and around the Lower Green Bay and Fox River Area of Concern (as designated by the Great Lakes Restoration Initiative). The data demonstrate longitudinal and lateral differences along the Lake Winnebago–Fox River–Green Bay continuum.

attracc.attraccr: Water quality and gas sensors were calibrated according to manufacturer protocols. Post hoc corrections were applied to carbon dioxide and methane values after analysis of gas standards.

procstep.procdesc: Step 1: Sensors were calibrated according to manufacturer protocols. Water sensors were outfitted with manufacturer provided flow cells. Dissolved gases were equilibrated in a flow-through sprayer chamber following procedures outlined in Loken and others, (2019). Water from 0.2 meter (m) depth was continuously pumped from the aft port side of the boat using a 5 gallon per minute (GPM) Shurflo Blaster II washdown pump. Water was routed through a size 50 mesh stainless steel screen and a series of Hayes automatic balancing valves to achieve a constant flow to the water quality sensors and gas equilibrator. 0.75 GPM of water was delivered to the seabird SUNA V2 optical nitrate sensor, then to the YSI EXO2, and then to a bbe fluoroprobe. The SUNA was kept in an ice bath to prevent overheating. On five of the eight campaigns, 3.0 GPM of water was delivered to a homemade gas sprayer (Loken and others, 2019), allowing dissolved gases to equilibrate in an enclosed headspace. Gases were recirculated to the Los Gatos Research Ultraportable Gas Analyzer (UGGA) using its internal pump at a flow rate of 0.8 standard pressure liters per minute (SPLM). Location was determined using a Garmin GPS 18X and a Garmin Echomap UHD. The Echomap transducer was mounted on the stern of the boat also capturing water temperature and depth to bottom. Barometric pressure was recorded with a Vaisala CS106 barometer. All data were captured continuously on a Campbell Scientific C6 datalogger and transmitted over Wi-Fi to an onboard computer for real-time acquisition and visualization.

Step 2: Data from the datalogger were processed using several established routines (Loken and others, 2019). First, “flame on” and “flame off” times were recorded to the second. Data outside these time intervals were excluded. Second, we applied post-calibration corrections for the SUNA and the UGGA. Prior to and after each campaign, we analyzed a set of nitrate, carbon dioxide, and methane standards to produce linear correction equations. The measured nitrate standard measurements were always within allowable ranges, and thus data from the SUNA were not adjusted. The UGGA tended to undermeasure the carbon dioxide and methane standards. We adjusted the reported carbon dioxide and methane data using linear regression equations from the check standards measured after each campaign. Third, for each variable (e.g., temperature), we replaced data with NA that were outside variable specific boundaries. For example, water temperature was required to be between 0 and 100 degrees Celsius. Fourth, we used the R package SensorQC to identify spurious values, which were converted to NA based on user-specified and variable-specific tolerances in rolling medians and rolling median absolute deviations.

Step 3: For each variable, we established a set of hydraulic and sensor response times to spatially correct the data. Essentially, the hydraulic-corrected data have been moved backwards in time and location to account for the travel time of water and gas through the series of pipes, tubing, pumps, regulators, and flow cells. Second, we applied a differential equation to account for sensor response dynamics, that adjusts the data for the amount of time for each flow cell to turnover and each sensor to stabilize. These methods are described in Crawford and others, 2015 and Loken and others, 2019. For each variable, we determined the specific hydraulic (hyd) and sensor response times (tau) using a series of step changes between known fluids in the laboratory. Columns ending in “_hyd" and “_tau” are the hydraulic- and tau-corrected (sensor response time) versions of each data variable.

Step 4: During each sampling campaign, we stopped the boat at ~30 locations to collect additional data. Field measurements and/or discrete samples were collected for lab analyses. During these discrete measurements and water collections, the boat stopped moving. The continuous, underway data were summarized to facilitate integration with field- and lab-based measurements. Associated with each discrete sample time, we calculated the median of 60 seconds of continuous data. For example, if a sample time was recorded as 10:00, the median values between 10:00:00 and 10:00:59 were calculated and associated with the discrete sample. These data are reported in the "FLAMe_Samples.csv" data table and can be joined to the lab- and field-based discrete measurements using the "lab_id" column.

overview.eaover: Data publication contains four files. 1. FLAMe_data.csv contains all continuous point measurements collected across the study. 2. Flame_sample.csv contains summarized sensor-based measurements associated with discrete water samples. 3. FLAMe_data_dictionary.csv contains details on data attributes including descriptions, units, sources and calculations. 4. FLAMe_map.png is an image of transect paths organized by campaign.
